title: Two suspects planning terror attack arrested in central Israel
description: Israel Police counterterrorism officers and Israel Security Agency (Shin Bet) operatives arrested two suspects involved in planning a terrorist attack against civilians, the agencies said in a joint statement on Monday night. Officers from the Border Police's Yamam National Counterterrorism Unit, acting on "precise intelligence" from the Shin Bet, located the suspects on Route 1 near the Latrun Interchange, some 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) west of Jerusalem, according to the statement. No Israeli security personnel were injured. The suspects were handed over to the Shin Bet for further questioning. The announcement came shortly after the police denied reports circulating on social media of a security incident near Teddy Stadium in southwestern Jerusalem. Police stressed there was "no unusual security incident" in the area and that the soccer match between Beitar Jerusalem and Maccabi Tel Aviv was continuing as usual. "We call on the public to rely on and heed official announcements from the Israel Police and the security forces, and to act responsibly when spreading information," the statement added. The rumors spread after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu canceled his visit to the match. Israeli Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir and several members of Netanyahu's Likud Party did attend, according to Israel Hayom .

title: French Jewish leader: Curfews have yet to restore confidence
description: France’s newly announced security measures have yet to restore confidence in authorities’ ability to contain rioting, a leader of the French Jewish community told JNS on Tuesday. “This week will be a very important week in order to know if the state takes back the power or not,” said Robert Ejnes, executive director of CRIF (Conseil Représentatif des Institutions Juives de France), the umbrella organization representing French-Jewish institutions. Asked whether he had confidence that authorities would be able to restore order in the face of the mass rioting, he said: “Not yet. We need to wait.” Bruno Benjamin, the head of the CRIF branch of Marseille-Provence this week urged French President Emmanuel Macron to declare a national state of emergency. On Monday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced “partial” and “localized” curfews following the weekend’s riots, in which at least 150 police officers were injured, according to Le Monde . The riots, which began last month ostensibly over poor conditions in French schools, have descended into violence against police, arson and vandalism, as well as widespread looting. Palestinian flags, in addition to Moroccan and Algerians ones, waved at protests have highlighted the role of immigrants from Muslim countries in the rioting. Benjamin accused the far-left France Unbowed party, or LFI, of orchestrating the riots, with help from people "who live in France, but hate France." Ejness said that the justice system’s handling of about 1,800 people who’d been arrested during the rioting in recent days was a major test for the state’s resolve to end the escalation. “We’re very eager to know now what will happen” to those arrested, he said, to establish “if the rule of law will prevail in France or whether these same people will be out by the next riot.” Lecornu appeared “determined” to stop the violence, Ejnes said, but added that a partial curfew offered only a temporary response. Ejnes also challenged claims circulating in Israel and on Jewish social media that rioters were systematically targeting Jewish businesses. Some Jewish-owned stores had suffered attacks, he said, but that alone did not establish an antisemitic motive. On Saturday night, a synagogue in the 19h Arrondissement of Paris was ransacked in an incident that Ejnes said did not feature any evidence of an antisemitic attack, and which seemed to suggest a robbery. Ejnes commented on a report Sunday by journalist Paul Amar of the Cnews television channel about a street in Marseille where only Jewish-owned stores hed been targeted. Ejnes said that he was aware of the report, but that it was not indicative of a phenomenon in which Jews are specifically targeted. Benjamin in Marseille told JNS the information reported by Cnews was “false.” The French-Jewish community’s security organization, SPCJ (Le Service de protection de la communauté juive ) , issued a statement saying it had no evidence that businesses had been attacked specifically because their owners were Jewish, Ejnes noted. That assessment offered no guarantee against future antisemitic attacks, Ejnes added. “We cannot be reassured that things will go well. We have to be realistic,” he said. “We have to raise the level of defense of the Jewish community, which is what we’re doing.”

title: Vance 'not getting involved in the Israeli elections' after Trump endorses Netanyahu
description: U.S. Vice President JD Vance said on Monday that he would be staying out of foreign elections when asked whether he would endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "This is the kind of partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel," Trump wrote, calling Netanyahu "strong, brave, and brilliant." Vance said he only endorses "American candidates." He added, "that's what I'm focused on" as the U.S. midterm elections approach. Asked directly whether he backed Netanyahu, Vance said, "I'm not anti-endorsing him; I'm not pro-endorsing him." In April, Vance made a two-day campaign visit to Hungary to back the reelection bid of former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. title: Narratives blaming Jews for French riots sweep X, report finds
description: Antisemitic sentiments on X following the civil unrest that recently erupted in France serve as another recurring example of online conspiracy theories blaming Jews and Israel for world events, according to a report released on Sunday by the Combat Antisemitism Movement’s (CAM) Antisemitism Research Center (ARC). Over a two-day period, the ARC documented 1,384 such posts from 816 unique accounts. The most common terminology variants included: Jewish elite orchestration, Israel/Mossad orchestration, Zionist manipulation, “Pro-Israel accounts are behind it,” Kalergi/Great Replacement, Rothschild/ZOG/money, and “Who benefits,” said CAM, a global coalition of interfaith organizations. The same pattern on X followed when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Ceuta, Spain, on July 30, 2026, according to CAM. Posts from 119 influencer accounts recast the border crisis as a Jewish plot, reaching an estimated 103 million people in 72 hours, ARC has found. When terrorists tried to hijack FlyDubai flight FZ1073 to Tel Aviv on Sept. 30, 2026, the first post blaming Israel appeared 67 minutes after the distress signal, CAM continued. The ARC collected 18,381 posts from X using 25 search queries in 7 languages. Any post linking the unrest in France to Jews, Israel, Zionists, or the Mossad was counted as antisemitic, according to CAM. Researchers read all 4,922 candidate text groups by hand and reviewed the 100 most-viewed posts individually.

title: After Trump threat, Araghchi warns Iran has unfinished business
description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Sunday that Tehran has "unfinished jobs" of its own, responding to U.S. President Donald Trump's threat to "finish the job" against the Islamic Republic. "Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too," Araghchi wrote on X, claiming his country had emerged stronger from the previous round of violence with Israel and the United States. He accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of pushing Washington toward another war "to stay out of jail, whatever the consequences for Israel—let alone POTUS." In a Truth Social post endorsing Netanyahu on Sunday, Trump warned that unless Tehran rapidly changes course, "we will soon finish the job." He then explicitly tied continued cooperation against the Islamic Republic to Netanyahu's political survival: "If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote. Last time you wanted to "finish the job", Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too. title: Huckabee opens first international Judea Conference in Hebron Hills
description: An international conference aimed at strengthening support for Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria opened on Sunday at the ancient site of Susya in the Hebron Hills, with U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee delivering the keynote address. The inaugural Judea Conference brings together Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Minister Amichai Chikli, ministry Director-General Avi Cohen-Scali, local council leaders, diplomats and representatives of international organizations. Huckabee’s appearance marked his first visit to the Hebron Hills. Organized by the Hebron Hills Regional Council’s International Desk in partnership with the Hebron Local Council, the conference aims to expand international ties with Jewish communities in the region and counter efforts to delegitimize Israel. “Hebron and its surrounding area are not only the cradle of the Jewish people’s history and identity, but also a strategic bridge to the entire world,” said Hebron Hills Regional Council head Eliram Azulay. Cohen-Scali said the ministry works with 12 local authorities in Judea and Samaria, providing advocacy tours and digital training programs. “We will continue to strengthen the region, support the local authorities in this vital struggle, and fight against delegitimization,” he said.

title: BBC AI specialist defended Hamas, served prison term, 'Telegraph' reports
description: A BBC specialist advising on artificial intelligence previously defended Hamas terrorism as “resistance” and served a prison sentence for immigration deception, Britain’s The Telegraph reported on Saturday. Hicham Yezza, principal data scientist in the broadcaster’s Responsible AI division, described Israel in a 2018 social media post as “an apartheid, nuclear-armed regime—one literally built on stolen land and ethnic cleansing.” In 2021, he characterized rocket attacks from Gaza as Palestinian efforts to “resist,” according to the report. The Algerian-born Yezza was sentenced to nine months in prison in 2009 for deceiving immigration authorities about his right to remain in Britain. He successfully appealed deportation in 2010 and is now a British citizen. He joined BBC Monitoring in 2021 before moving into his current role, helping guide the broadcaster’s use of AI. The BBC said Yezza had not breached its social media policies while employed by the broadcaster and had stopped working for Ceasefire , the pro-Palestinian magazine he founded, when he joined the corporation. “While we wouldn’t normally comment on individuals, none of this appears to relate to his time at the BBC,” a spokesman said.

description: Haifa-based Elbit Systems said on Monday it was awarded a contract worth about $235 million to supply rockets and artillery launchers to an unnamed European country under an agreement between Israel’s Defense Ministry and its counterpart in the customer country. The contract will be carried out over three years and includes EXTRA-MR medium-range rockets, PULS rocket artillery launchers, additional rocket-artillery platforms and logistics support. The EXTRA-MR is a precision-guided variant of Elbit’s EXTRA supersonic rocket system, with a range of up to 80 kilometers (about 50 miles). It is compatible with the Israeli defense firm's PULS launchers and existing command-and-control systems. "This contract award further strengthens Elbit Systems’ position as a global leader in rocket artillery systems and reflects the growing international demand for our advanced rocket and launcher capabilities," said Elbit President and CEO Bezhalel Machlis. "The PULS systems and precision rocket solutions are recognized among the leading systems in their category and have been selected by a growing number of customers worldwide, including European and NATO member states. We remain committed to delivering advanced operational capabilities that support our customers’ evolving defense requirements." title: Is Jewish unity in a polarized nation possible?
description: At a time when most Americans have lost the ability to listen to people with opposing views on political issues, how can a fractious Jewish community that is also split on denominational lines pull together? That’s the question posed by JNS editor-in-chief Jonathan Tobin. He believes that Jewish disunity has been exacerbated by the capture of the political left, which is still supported by the majority of Jews, by anti-Israel and antisemitic “progressives.” This puts even more pressure on Jewish liberals to conform to fashionable opinion on the left that poses a threat to their community’s interests and safety. He’s joined in this week’s episode of “Think Twice” by DePaul University Law professor Roberta Kwall, author of the new book , Polarized: Why American Jews Are Divided And What to Do About It . She believes that a vital Jewish center can be reconstituted if people realize that what unites them is still greater than those who seek to tear them apart. Part of the problem is that Israel, which was once thought to be a unifying factor, is now the greatest source of division, with many unaffiliated or liberal Jews no longer supportive of it, and a small but well-publicized minority actively opposed to Zionism. At the core of her effort is a statement of largely anodyne principles that she believes the overwhelming majority of Jews agree on. Among them is support for the right of Israel to exist as a Jewish and democratic state, as well as the legitimacy of criticizing its government. But for Kwall, equally important is the need to re-emphasize education and the importance of tradition to reinforce Jewish identity. In such a context, it will be easier for Jews who disagree on politics or aspects of Israeli policy to listen to each other and find common ground. title: Israeli engineering team makes history at Europe’s 24-hour solar car race
description: A team of engineering students from Afeka Academic College of Engineering in Tel Aviv made history this month, becoming the first Israeli team to compete in the iLumen European Solar Challenge in Belgium, a 24-hour solar-powered endurance race. Competing as AFEKA Racing, the students completed 197 laps—nearly 800 kilometers (490 miles)—in a solar-powered vehicle they designed and built themselves, finishing 14th overall and ranking first among the six teams competing in the challenge for the first time. The race marked the culmination of an ambitious multidisciplinary project bringing together Afeka students from mechanical, electrical, software and industrial engineering. Working across disciplines, the students combined their expertise to design and build a functioning solar race car capable of competing on the international stage. Completing a 24-hour solar endurance race tested not only the vehicle’s design and performance but also the students’ ability to solve engineering problems in real time under demanding race conditions. Over the course of the competition, the team confronted technical challenges including communication issues with the vehicle’s computer system and higher-than-expected tire wear, even performing a wheel alignment during the race to keep the car moving. “What made me most proud was seeing how the team grew throughout the project,” said Dr. Dan Herman, who leads Afeka’s Auto Club. “At the beginning, I was deeply involved in managing the project and making decisions. Over time, the students took ownership, managed themselves and learned to make those decisions together. Even when we faced challenges during the race, they worked as a team, solved every problem and kept the car moving.” Afeka is the only academic institution in Israel to offer an automotive specialization as part of its undergraduate mechanical engineering program. The solar car project builds on that focus by taking engineering education beyond the classroom and giving students hands-on experience designing and constructing a complex vehicle while collaborating across engineering disciplines. This approach extends across Afeka’s student engineering clubs, which give students opportunities to apply their knowledge across disciplines and take on ambitious real-world engineering challenges. The team sees its participation in Belgium as a foundation for the continued development of Afeka’s solar racing program. The project is designed to grow from one generation of Afeka engineers to the next. Current and future students will build on the knowledge developed by the team, while Auto Club alumni look forward to remaining involved, sharing their experience and contributing to the project even after graduation. “Engineering education is at its best when students have the opportunity to take what they learn in the classroom and apply it to complex, real-world challenges,” said Prof. Yossi Rosenwaks, president of Afeka Academic College of Engineering. “What these students accomplished in Belgium reflects the creativity, determination and interdisciplinary collaboration we strive to cultivate at Afeka. More importantly, it reflects the kind of engineers we seek to educate — engineers who can turn knowledge into action, take on ambitious challenges and help shape Israel’s technological future . We are incredibly proud of the way they represented Afeka and Israel on the international stage, and we look forward to seeing how they build on this achievement in the years ahead.” The team is already looking toward an even larger challenge: the Bridgestone World Solar Challenge in Australia, one of the world’s leading solar vehicle competitions. AFEKA Racing hopes to use the experience gained in Belgium as a foundation for bringing an Afeka-built solar car to the competition, which will take place in August 2027 and send teams on a roughly 3,000-kilometer journey from Darwin to Adelaide.

title: Three principles behind the secret to the IDF’s success can change your life
description: The secret to the success of the Israel Defense Forces can be credited to a number of factors; according to JNS Israel military correspondent Yaakov Lappin, however, it involves creating a culture as much as the courage of its soldiers, air crews and sailors, and their effective use of cutting-edge technology. Lappin, who has written about this in his recently published book, Blue Team Dynamics: Three Proven Leadership Principles Inspired by IDF Sources for Business and Life , joins JNS editor-in-chief Jonathan Tobin on this week’s episode of “Think Twice” to discuss how this works. The book is based on years of research and interviews dating back to 2018. According to Lappin, the three principles that are the foundation of IDF culture involve the importance of after-action review of everything they do; cultivating the ability to switch from the routine to an emergency mode; and encouraging the need to recognize how to manage long-term change inside an organization. As he notes, the same ideas can help individuals or non-military organizations and businesses also succeed. Lappin concedes that many of these lessons were forgotten by Israel’s military and intelligence establishment as well as their political masters before the catastrophe of Oct. 7, 2023, which occurred almost exactly 50 years after the IDF suffered another disaster that was also rooted in organizational failure. With respect to Oct. 7, he says the mistake came from a basic human failing in which, “the human mind adopts and falls in love with a narrative” that is very difficult to break out of. This overrode the culture that should have prevented the complacency that led to the Hamas and Palestinian terrorists being able to carry out the worst mass slaughter of Jews since the Holocaust. Prioritizing after-action detailed post-training and combat analysis started inside the Israeli Air Force, but it has spread to the other branches of the military now as well. That involves creating a culture where admitting mistakes of any kind is not only permitted but lauded as necessary, especially where it concerns commanders. The necessity of knowing when to switch to emergency mode was actually highlighted by the way many in the IDF responded to Oct. 7. Those efforts ensured that the grievous damage inflicted by Hamas was limited and then allowed the Israelis to defeat the terrorists. Nevertheless, it’s still true that the IDF failed to anticipate this “black swan” event and that the procedures that should have prevented that mistake, which involve looking for “black feathers,” rather than the swan itself, didn’t happen. According to Lappin, the “Blue Team” approach, which refers to the creation of two groups dedicated to both planning IDF actions and those that seek to examine and defeat those plans as an enemy would, must also be credited for the amazing triumphs Israel achieved after Oct. 7 in Lebanon and against Iran. And as he notes, the very same ideas have been applied by IDF veterans in their post-military careers in business and technology.
